E.11 Which frictions matter? Experiments

Chapter 15 explained each pattern with one friction: sticky prices for the fall in hours after a TFP shock, sticky wages for the fall in the real wage after a monetary expansion, investment adjustment costs for the large fall in consumption after a monetary tightening. In a model with all frictions at once, we can test these explanations: we change one parameter, solve the model again, and compare. The function experiment does this for a list of values.

def experiment(parameter, values, shock, size):
    """Impulse responses to one shock for several values of one parameter; returns a list of runs."""
    colors, runs = [BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY], []
    for j, value in enumerate(values):
        model = load_sw({parameter: value}, file="sw_experiment.yaml")
        label = f"{parameter} = {value}" + (" (estimate)" if abs(value - SW_MODE[parameter]) < 0.01 else "")
        runs.append((label, irf(model, shock, size), colors[j], "-" if j == 0 else "--"))
    return runs

def peaks(runs, columns, T=20):
    """The largest response (in absolute value) of each column within T quarters, for each run."""
    rows = {}
    for label, table, color, style in runs:
        part = table[columns].iloc[:T]
        rows[label] = [part[c][part[c].abs().idxmax()] for c in columns]
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, index=[f"largest {c}" for c in columns]).T.round(2)

Python note. enumerate(values) gives each value together with its position j, which we use to pick a color. part[c].abs().idxmax() is the quarter in which the response is largest in absolute value, so that peaks reports falls as negative numbers and rises as positive ones.

Fig. 9: Sticky prices and the fall in hours after a TFP shock

The textbook explains the fall in hours after a TFP shock by sticky prices: demand rises slowly, and firms with higher productivity need fewer workers to meet it. If that is the whole story, hours should rise when prices are flexible. We lower the Calvo parameter \(\xi_p\) from its estimate, 0.66 (prices last about three quarters on average, \(1/(1-\xi_p)\)), to 0.1, and add the model’s own flexible economy, which has flexible prices and wages.

runs = experiment("cprobp", [0.6563, 0.5, 0.3, 0.1], "ea", 1.0)
panels = [("GDP", "GDP"), ("hours", "Hours worked"), ("inflation", "Inflation"), ("real wage", "Real wage")]
four_panels(runs, "Less sticky prices raise GDP faster after a TFP shock, but hours still fall at first",
            "Impulse responses to a TFP shock for four values of the Calvo price parameter: GDP rises faster and "
            "inflation falls more when prices are less sticky; hours fall at first in every case", panels=panels)

# The flexible economy is part of every solution: its GDP and hours are the columns "flexible-price ..."
flex = tfp.copy()
flex["GDP"], flex["hours"] = tfp["flexible-price GDP"], tfp["flexible-price hours"]
table = peaks(runs + [("flexible prices and wages", flex, RUST, ":")], ["GDP", "hours"])
table["hours in quarter 1"] = [run[1]["hours"][1] for run in runs] + [flex["hours"][1]]
table.round(2)
largest GDP largest hours hours in quarter 1
cprobp = 0.6563 (estimate) 1.49 -0.63 -0.63
cprobp = 0.5 1.64 -0.60 -0.60
cprobp = 0.3 1.80 -0.57 -0.57
cprobp = 0.1 1.93 -0.52 -0.52
flexible prices and wages 1.59 -0.43 -0.43

Source. Computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007); related to Fig. 10 of Chapter 15 and to Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed..

What to notice. Less sticky prices make GDP rise faster and inflation fall more, as Chapter 15 predicts. But hours fall at first in every case, even in the flexible economy (the last line of the table). In the Smets–Wouters model, sticky prices make the fall in hours larger and longer, but they are not its only cause: with habits and investment adjustment costs, demand also rises slowly in a flexible economy, and a richer household wants to work less. The next cell switches those two real frictions off as well.

no_frictions = {"cprobp": 0.1, "cprobw": 0.3, "chabb": 0.1, "csadjcost": 2.0}
runs_real = [("estimated model", tfp, BLUE, "-"),
             ("flexible prices and wages", irf(load_sw({"cprobp": 0.1, "cprobw": 0.3}), "ea", 1.0), TEAL, "--"),
             ("... and weak habits and adjustment costs", irf(load_sw(no_frictions), "ea", 1.0), GREEN, "--")]
table = peaks(runs_real, ["GDP", "hours"])
table["hours in quarter 1"] = [run[1]["hours"][1] for run in runs_real]
table["hours in quarter 2"] = [run[1]["hours"][2] for run in runs_real]
table.round(2)
largest GDP largest hours hours in quarter 1 hours in quarter 2
estimated model 1.49 -0.63 -0.63 -0.43
flexible prices and wages 1.65 -0.54 -0.54 -0.27
... and weak habits and adjustment costs 1.83 -0.15 -0.15 0.07

What to notice. Only when the nominal and the real frictions are weak does the fall in hours almost vanish: hours fall by about 0.15 percent in the first quarter and rise from the second. The textbook’s simple labor market, with no habits and no adjustment costs, is close to this last case. Which frictions are strong in the real economy is exactly what estimation decides, and the estimated frictions make hours fall. Whether they do in the data is, as the textbook says, still debated.

Fig. 10: Sticky wages and the real wage after a monetary shock

Chapter 15 showed that with sticky nominal wages, a monetary shock moves the real wage against employment. We vary the Calvo parameter of wages \(\xi_w\).

runs = experiment("cprobw", [0.7375, 0.5, 0.3], "em", 0.25)
panels = [("GDP", "GDP"), ("hours", "Hours worked"), ("inflation", "Inflation"), ("real wage", "Real wage")]
four_panels(runs, "With more flexible wages, a monetary tightening lowers inflation and the real wage more",
            "Impulse responses to a monetary policy shock for three values of the Calvo wage parameter: "
            "with more flexible wages inflation and the real wage fall more, and GDP and hours a little less",
            panels=panels)
peaks(runs, ["GDP", "hours", "inflation", "real wage"])
largest GDP largest hours largest inflation largest real wage
cprobw = 0.7375 (estimate) -0.35 -0.23 -0.20 -0.14
cprobw = 0.5 -0.32 -0.19 -0.30 -0.29
cprobw = 0.3 -0.31 -0.17 -0.35 -0.43

Source. Computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007); related to Figs. 6 and 7 of Chapter 15 and to Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed..

What to notice. At the estimate, a tightening lowers the real wage only a little, and slowly: nominal wages are sticky, and so are prices. With more flexible wages, the real wage falls more, which makes marginal cost (E.7) and inflation fall more, and GDP and hours a little less. More flexible wages make the economy adjust through prices rather than quantities. In this model prices are sticky too, so the real wage falls with employment, unlike the sticky-wage-only case of Chapter 15, Fig. 7: both nominal frictions together decide its sign.

Fig. 11: Habits, investment costs and consumption after a monetary shock

Jones (2024) explains the large fall in consumption after a monetary tightening by investment adjustment costs. We test it: first we change the adjustment cost \(\varphi\), then the habit parameter \(h\).

runs_phi = experiment("csadjcost", [5.4882, 2.0, 10.0], "em", 0.25)
runs_h = experiment("chabb", [0.7124, 0.4, 0.1], "em", 0.25)
panels = [("GDP", "GDP"), ("consumption", "Consumption"), ("investment", "Investment"), ("hours", "Hours worked")]
four_panels(runs_h, "Weaker habits make consumption fall more, and sooner, after a monetary tightening",
            "Impulse responses to a monetary policy shock for three values of the habit parameter: with weaker "
            "habits consumption and GDP fall more at once", panels=panels)
pd.concat([peaks(runs_phi, ["GDP", "consumption", "investment"]), peaks(runs_h, ["GDP", "consumption", "investment"])])
largest GDP largest consumption largest investment
csadjcost = 5.4882 (estimate) -0.35 -0.35 -0.58
csadjcost = 2.0 -0.45 -0.35 -1.08
csadjcost = 10.0 -0.32 -0.35 -0.38
chabb = 0.7124 (estimate) -0.35 -0.35 -0.58
chabb = 0.4 -0.44 -0.49 -0.73
chabb = 0.1 -0.49 -0.60 -0.80

Source. Computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007); related to Chapter 15 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed..

What to notice. The adjustment cost changes the response of investment a lot (it falls about twice as much with \(\varphi = 2\) as at the estimate), but the largest fall in consumption hardly changes. The habit parameter changes the consumption response: with \(h = 0.1\), consumption falls by about 0.6 percent at once, against 0.2 at the estimate, and its trough comes at once instead of after a year. So in this model, habits shape the consumption response, and adjustment costs the investment response. Consumption falls about as much as GDP because GDP falls less: investment, held back by its adjustment costs, falls only about 0.6 percent, and capacity utilization absorbs part of the shock.

Fig. 12: The Taylor rule

The response of monetary policy shapes every impulse response. We vary the response to inflation \(r_\pi\) and the interest-rate smoothing \(\rho\).

runs_pi = experiment("crpi", [2.0295, 1.5, 3.0], "em", 0.25)
runs_rho = experiment("crr", [0.8153, 0.5, 0.0], "em", 0.25)
panels = [("GDP", "GDP"), ("inflation", "Inflation"), ("interest rate", "Interest rate"), ("consumption", "Consumption")]
four_panels(runs_rho, "Without interest-rate smoothing, a policy surprise is over in a quarter",
            "Impulse responses to a monetary policy shock for three values of the smoothing parameter: with less "
            "smoothing the rate falls back at once and GDP, consumption and inflation barely move", panels=panels)
pd.concat([peaks(runs_pi, ["GDP", "inflation"]), peaks(runs_rho, ["GDP", "inflation"])])
largest GDP largest inflation
crpi = 2.0295 (estimate) -0.35 -0.20
crpi = 1.5 -0.41 -0.26
crpi = 3.0 -0.30 -0.14
crr = 0.8153 (estimate) -0.35 -0.20
crr = 0.5 -0.12 -0.04
crr = 0.0 -0.05 -0.01

Source. Computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007); related to Chapters 12 and 13 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed..

What to notice. Smoothing does most of the work. With \(\rho = 0.82\), a surprise keeps the funds rate high for about a year, and it is the expected path of rates, not one quarter’s rate, that moves consumption and investment through (E.2)–(E.4). Without smoothing, the rate is back to normal in the next quarter and GDP falls by only about 0.05 percent. A stronger response to inflation (\(r_\pi = 3\)) makes the fall in inflation and GDP smaller: people know that the bank will push inflation back hard, so it moves less in the first place.

Your turn. Combine the two cases of Fig. 9. Which friction, on its own, removes most of the fall in hours after a TFP shock: flexible prices (cprobp = 0.1), weak habits (chabb = 0.1), or low adjustment costs (csadjcost = 2)?

Show the answer 
for change in [{"cprobp": 0.1}, {"chabb": 0.1}, {"csadjcost": 2.0}]:
    hours = irf(load_sw(change), "ea", 1.0)["hours"]
    print(change, f"hours in quarter 1: {hours[1]:.2f}%, quarter 4: {hours[4]:.2f}%")

Each change on its own leaves a fall in hours in the first quarter; none removes it. Weak habits do the most (hours fall by about 0.3 percent instead of 0.6), flexible prices less, and low adjustment costs almost nothing. The frictions reinforce each other: demand rises slowly when any of them is strong, so the fall in hours almost disappears only when all are weak.

# Your turn: try it here

E.12 The file’s own numbers, and the corrected equation

How much did our two changes to the file matter? We compare four versions for the monetary policy and the investment-specific shocks: the published estimates with and without the corrected equation (E.6), and the file’s own calibration.

def load_file_calibration(fixed):
    """The file as shipped (its own calibration), without the estimation block."""
    d = yaml.safe_load(text); d.pop("estimated_parameters")
    if fixed:
        eqs = "\n".join(d["equations"])
        for old, new in FIX:
            eqs = eqs.replace(old, new)
        d["equations"] = eqs.split("\n")
    path = os.path.join(WORK, "sw_file.yaml")
    with open(path, "w") as f:
        yaml.safe_dump(d, f, sort_keys=False, width=10_000)
    model, report = quietly(driver.importModel, fname=path, Solver="AndersonMoore")
    return model

versions = {"estimates, corrected (E.6)": sw,
            "estimates, as published": load_sw(fixed=False, file="sw_published.yaml"),
            "file's calibration, corrected": load_file_calibration(True)}
rows = {}
for name, model in versions.items():
    m_irf, i_irf = irf(model, "em", 0.25), irf(model, "eqs", SW_SD["eqs"])
    rows[name] = {"GDP after monetary shock": m_irf["GDP"].iloc[:20].min(),
                  "inflation after monetary shock": m_irf["inflation"].iloc[:20].min(),
                  "GDP after investment shock": i_irf["GDP"].iloc[:20].max(),
                  "investment after investment shock": i_irf["investment"].iloc[:20].max()}
pd.DataFrame(rows).T.round(3)
GDP after monetary shock inflation after monetary shock GDP after investment shock investment after investment shock
estimates, corrected (E.6) -0.354 -0.198 0.581 3.129
estimates, as published -0.354 -0.198 0.569 3.169
file's calibration, corrected -0.593 -0.407 0.821 3.391 
file_mp = irf(versions["file's calibration, corrected"], "em", 0.25)
four_panels([("published estimates", mp, BLUE, "-"), ("the file's own calibration", file_mp, TEAL, "--")],
            "The file's calibration makes a monetary shock almost twice as strong",
            "Impulse responses to a monetary policy shock with the published estimates and with the file's own "
            "calibration: the falls in GDP, consumption, hours and inflation are much larger with the file's values")

Source. Computed with the model file of the Snowdrop package and the estimates of Smets and Wouters (2007); related to Chapter 15 of Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed..

What to notice. The corrected equation changes only the responses to the investment-specific shock, by a few percent: it multiplies only that shock. The calibration matters much more: with the file’s values, the same monetary shock lowers GDP by almost twice as much. A file with the right equations and the wrong numbers gives confident, wrong answers. Before you use a model file, compare its numbers with the source it claims to follow.

E.13 Go further

Estimating the model

Appendix D.11–D.12 estimated a three-equation model. The same steps estimate this one: the seven observed series, measurement equations (the file’s measurement_equations block links them to the model), priors (Table 1 of the paper, or the file’s estimated_parameters block, rewritten in Snowdrop’s layout) and Snowdrop’s estimate. The data are in the replication files of Smets and Wouters (2007) and in Pfeifer’s collection of Dynare models; the FRED series can be downloaded with the tools of Appendix B. Expect a long computation: 36 parameters and a flat likelihood in some directions.

Where the equations come from

The log-linear equations of Section E.3 are derived in Smets and Wouters (2007, Section I and the online appendix) and, step by step, in Galí (2015, for the simpler New Keynesian model) and in the notes of Del Negro and Schorfheide (2012). Christiano, Eichenbaum and Evans (2005) explain why each friction is there: they choose them to match the responses of the U.S. economy to a monetary policy shock estimated without a model.

Common errors and how to fix them

What you see Why What to do
could not convert string to float: 'inv_gamma_pdf' the file’s estimation block has a layout that Snowdrop does not read remove the block, as write_sw does
a chart that looks plausible but a residual of 0.02 the Klein solver fails on this model in this version of Snowdrop Solver="AndersonMoore"; always check the residuals
Python stops with “unable to find solution” the Villemot solver fails on this model use Anderson–Moore or Binder–Pesaran
a parameter change has no effect the derived values (cbetabar, ccy, …) were computed when the file was read write the file again with load_sw({...})
the risk premium shock has the wrong sign or size the file’s b is \(-c_3\varepsilon^b\) a rise in the premium of \(x\) points is b \(= -c_3x\)
responses four times too small or too large inflation and the interest rate are quarterly in the model multiply by 4 for annual rates, as irf does
a crash after changing a Calvo parameter to 0 or 1 \(\xi\) appears in a denominator use values strictly between 0 and 1

Concluding remarks

  • The Smets–Wouters model puts the pieces of Chapter 15 together, with habits, investment adjustment costs, variable capacity utilization, sticky prices and wages with indexation, a Taylor rule on the output gap and seven shocks. Its 14 equations are log-linear: each one is a weighted average whose weights come from the deep parameters.
  • Snowdrop solves it in a fraction of a second, but only one of its linear solvers gives the right answer for this model: checking the residuals found the problem.
  • With the published estimates, the model reproduces the textbook’s responses to a monetary policy shock, a TFP shock and a rise in government purchases, almost number for number. The financial friction shock matches once its units are understood.
  • Experiments show that the frictions work together. The fall in hours after a TFP shock comes from sticky prices and from real frictions; habits shape the response of consumption to monetary policy, and adjustment costs that of investment; interest-rate smoothing carries most of the effect of a policy surprise.
  • Research files must be read with care. The model file differs from the paper in its numbers, in one equation and in the units of one shock, and each difference changes the answers.
